sources.title: Ronald de Wolf, Quantum Computing: Lecture Notes, arXiv:1907.09415v6 (2026-08-27)
sources.locator: Chapter 2, §2.4 (including §§2.4.1–2.4.2), PDF pp.29–32 (printed pp.17–20): XOR and phase queries; Deutsch–Jozsa and Bernstein–Vazirani algorithms, amplitudes, and classical query comparisons.

contents.name: Hadamard character sum on F_2^n
contents.reason: The section gives the binary Hadamard phase expansion and mod-two inner product; the carrier supplies the complete coordinate factorization proof.

contents.name: Deutsch constant-versus-balanced promise
contents.reason: The two-point Deutsch promise is the n=1 constant-versus-balanced case of the query setup.

contents.name: Deutsch–Jozsa promise
contents.reason: The section states the constant-or-balanced promise, one-query Hadamard procedure, zero-frequency amplitude, and exact output rule.

contents.name: Bernstein–Vazirani no-offset promise
contents.reason: The section states the no-offset inner-product promise and proves exact one-query recovery from the Hadamard transform.

contents.name: One classical query cannot solve Deutsch exactly
contents.reason: The source establishes the oracle/query model; the one-bit randomized 1/2 worst-case bound is proved directly from the four truth tables.

contents.name: Exact deterministic Deutsch–Jozsa needs N/2+1 queries
contents.reason: The source gives the deterministic N/2+1 lower bound; the carrier supplies the adaptive-transcript completion proof and matching upper bound.

contents.name: Three classical samples solve Deutsch–Jozsa with bounded error
contents.reason: The source gives a different two-random-query procedure with 1/2 success on balanced inputs; it does not prove the planned three-distinct-sample 3/4 bound, which is proved locally by finite counting.

contents.name: Classical Bernstein–Vazirani needs n queries for bounded error
contents.reason: The source states the n-query information requirement; the item proves the sharper explicit 2^{q−n} average-success bound by a decision-tree leaf count.

contents.name: One-query Deutsch algorithm
contents.reason: The section gives the one-query interference construction; our carrier fixes zero initialization and counts each X/H gate.

contents.name: One-query Deutsch–Jozsa algorithm
contents.reason: The section states the constant-or-balanced promise, one-query Hadamard procedure, zero-frequency amplitude, and exact output rule.

contents.name: One-query Bernstein–Vazirani algorithm
contents.reason: The section states the no-offset inner-product promise and proves exact one-query recovery from the Hadamard transform.

contents.name: Deutsch algorithm is exact
contents.reason: The section gives the one-query interference construction; our carrier fixes zero initialization and counts each X/H gate.

contents.name: Deutsch–Jozsa algorithm is exact
contents.reason: The section states the constant-or-balanced promise, one-query Hadamard procedure, zero-frequency amplitude, and exact output rule.

contents.name: Bernstein–Vazirani algorithm returns the secret exactly
contents.reason: The section states the no-offset inner-product promise and proves exact one-query recovery from the Hadamard transform.

sources.title: John Preskill, Quantum Information, Chapter 6: Quantum Algorithms (updated November 2020)
sources.locator: §6.1, PDF pp.8–11 (printed pp.2–5): Deutsch, Deutsch–Jozsa, and Bernstein–Vazirani promises, output amplitudes, and classical query discussion.

contents.name: Hadamard character sum on F_2^n
contents.reason: Equations (6.8)–(6.9) give H^{⊗n} amplitudes and the bitwise mod-two dot product; the carrier proves the finite character sum locally.

contents.name: Deutsch constant-versus-balanced promise
contents.reason: Section 6.1 states the two-point constant-versus-balanced promise.

contents.name: Deutsch–Jozsa promise
contents.reason: Section 6.1 derives the constant-or-balanced promise and the one-query output amplitude.

contents.name: Bernstein–Vazirani no-offset promise
contents.reason: Section 6.1 states the inner-product promise and derives the exact one-query secret output.

contents.name: One classical query cannot solve Deutsch exactly
contents.reason: The source gives the two-point query setting; the local proof establishes the exact two-query count and randomized 1/2 worst-case bound.

contents.name: Exact deterministic Deutsch–Jozsa needs N/2+1 queries
contents.reason: Section 6.1 gives the exact-certainty cutoff; the local proof supplies both adversarial completion and matching algorithm.

contents.name: Three classical samples solve Deutsch–Jozsa with bounded error
contents.reason: The source discusses a prior-weighted stopping procedure, not this fixed three-sample worst-case guarantee; the item proves the without-replacement probability directly.

contents.name: Classical Bernstein–Vazirani needs n queries for bounded error
contents.reason: The source notes that n classical bits must be learned; the item gives the complete adaptive decision-tree and random-tape proof.

contents.name: One-query Deutsch algorithm
contents.reason: Section 6.1 directly derives the two-point circuit and its deterministic measured output.

contents.name: One-query Deutsch–Jozsa algorithm
contents.reason: Section 6.1 derives the constant-or-balanced promise and the one-query output amplitude.

contents.name: One-query Bernstein–Vazirani algorithm
contents.reason: Section 6.1 states the inner-product promise and derives the exact one-query secret output.

contents.name: Deutsch algorithm is exact
contents.reason: Section 6.1 directly derives the two-point circuit and its deterministic measured output.

contents.name: Deutsch–Jozsa algorithm is exact
contents.reason: Section 6.1 derives the constant-or-balanced promise and the one-query output amplitude.

contents.name: Bernstein–Vazirani algorithm returns the secret exactly
contents.reason: Section 6.1 states the inner-product promise and derives the exact one-query secret output.
